analysis.one_liner: Creates a universal, state-run national health plan covering hospital, doctor, mental health, and long-term care with capped out-of-pocket costs.
analysis.headline: The universal health plan never got a vote: after introduction it sat in two House committees and their health subcommittees for the full two-year Congress, with 24 House Democratic sponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made every U.S. resident eligible to enroll in a state-run health plan offering hospital care, physician services, preventive care, mental health and substance abuse treatment, and long-term care. Federal and state money would flow to state Comprehensive Health Care Funds, which would pay approved health plans a fixed monthly amount per enrollee. Cost-sharing would be capped — $500 family deductible, 20% coinsurance, and nothing at all for families under 200% of the poverty line — and private insurance would be barred from selling coverage that duplicates the basic benefit package. Hospitals would be paid under state-set prospective budgets and doctors under negotiated fee schedules, accepting the plan payment as payment in full.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 35 million uninsured Americans of the era plus everyone facing large medical bills: all lawful residents would be enrolled, providers would have to accept plan payment as payment in full, and families below twice the poverty line would owe nothing in premiums or cost-sharing. The long-term care title would pay for home and community-based care, the first six months of nursing home care, and respite care for family caregivers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured and underinsured Americans of all ages

how_it_helps.text: Makes every citizen, national, and lawful resident alien eligible to enroll in a qualified health plan in their state, with automatic default enrollment when care is first provided [S3].

Requires plans to cover hospital care, physician and professional services, diagnostic tests, prenatal and well-baby care, mental health services, substance abuse treatment, hospice, and preventive services including annual mammography [S3].
Bans cost-sharing entirely for families with income below 200% of the poverty line and caps family out-of-pocket costs at $500 deductible, 20% coinsurance, and $2,500 total per year [S3].
Requires providers to accept the plan's payment as payment in full, so no balance billing above the allowed cost-sharing [S3].

Creates a Lifecare Long-Term Care Protection Program paying for home and community-based care, the first six months of nursing home care, and up to 30 days of respite care for family caregivers, with an optional federal insurance program for longer stays [S3].
Bars private insurance from selling coverage duplicating the basic benefits, ending duplicative private premiums for coverage the public plan already provides [S3].
Authorizes additional research funding for AIDS, hypertension, sickle cell anemia, infant mortality, and breast cancer, plus grants for public health planning and geriatric training [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal and state taxpayers would finance the program through a national health budget and required state contributions, and enrollees could still owe premiums, deductibles, and coinsurance up to the caps. Health insurers would lose the ability to sell duplicative basic coverage, hospitals would submit to biennial state-set budgets and possible bed reductions, and physicians would accept negotiated fee schedules with mandatory assignment.

drawbacks.text: The program would only take effect if at least half the states enacted implementing legislation first, and each state would have to enroll 90% of eligible residents to be considered operational — a structure that could leave the promise unfulfilled [S3].
States may still charge premiums and cost-sharing up to the caps, so coverage would not be free for most working families, and cost-sharing could reach $2,500 per family per year [S3].
Mental health coverage is limited to 45 inpatient days or 20 outpatient visits per year, and states may further limit substance abuse treatment [S3].
Basic benefits mirror Medicare's exclusions: dental care, eyeglasses, routine physicals outside preventive services, and cosmetic surgery would not be covered [S3].

Biennial prospective budgets and state commissions to reduce excess hospital beds would mean hard spending limits on hospitals, which supporters saw as cost control and critics saw as rationing risk [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside was large and concrete — universal enrollment, an end to balance billing, real out-of-pocket caps, and a national long-term care benefit. The costs were also real: substantial new federal and state spending, and strict payment controls on hospitals and doctors whose effectiveness was unproven at scale. The design's weakest point is its trigger: nothing would have happened unless half the states legislated first, which in practice made the guarantee conditional. It died before any of this could be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees on the day it was introduced, then to their health subcommittees, and no committee or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Mary Rose Oakar introduced the bill on January 3, 1991, the first day of the 102nd Congress; it was referred jointly to the Committees on Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means [S5].
On January 23, 1991 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and on February 11, 1991 to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote. The bill died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5].
The bill's sponsors grew from the original eight to 24 House members over 1991, all Democrats; no Republican ever sponsored or cosponsored it [S3].
The early-1990s Congress took up many competing health reform proposals; this one, one of the broadest universal plans, never advanced past subcommittee referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, hospitals, and physician groups were better off because the bill died — they avoided mandatory assignment, state-set budgets, bed-reduction commissions, and a ban on selling duplicative private coverage. The tens of millions of Americans then without coverage or facing uncapped bills gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, hospitals, and physicians; the uninsured gained nothing

against.role: Insurers selling employer and individual coverage
against.what_they_did: Opposed universal-coverage proposals of this era that would bar private plans from duplicating basic coverage, in public testimony and lobbying against the 1991-94 reform debate

sides.party_line_note: All 24 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a vote, so no bipartisan support ever materialized.

industries.note: The bill bans any private insurance that duplicates the basic benefit package, so insurers could no longer sell the coverage most working households buy today; they would survive only as state-approved health plans paid fixed per-enrollee amounts.

Hospitals would be paid under biennial prospective budgets negotiated with each state, and states must create commissions to reduce excess beds with plans to refinance debt and retrain displaced staff.
Doctors would accept plan payment as payment in full under fee schedules set by state boards on a national relative value scale, eliminating balance billing.

industries.industry: Home care and long-term care providers
industries.note: The Lifecare program would route federal payments to certified home health agencies, home care agencies, and adult day health centers for millions of newly eligible clients, with federal grants for training the workforce.
